title: Why We Don't Talk About Summative and Formative Assessment
author: Becky Allen and Matthew Evans
summary: Becky Allen and Matthew Evans argue that the standard division of school assessments into 'formative' (assessment for learning) and 'summative' (assessment of learning) is conceptually flawed and produces bad practice. Drawing on Dylan Wiliam's point that formative and summative describe how an assessment is used rather than what it is, they push further: every assessment must be both formative and summative, because all assessments involve making inferences about what a student can do, and all should ultimately serve learning. They identify four specific ways the false dichotomy distorts practice -- treating high-stakes tests as purely bureaucratic rather than learning-supportive, assuming accuracy matters more for summative than formative assessment, oversimplifying which assessment formats suit big versus small tests, and assuming relative attainment measurement only matters for big tests. The authors close by pointing to AI-driven platforms like Sparx Maths and Duolingo, which continuously assess and shape learning simultaneously, as evidence that the formative/summative label has become genuinely meaningless in an AI-assisted assessment landscape.
points: The authors' core reframe -- 'all assessments must be both formative and summative, or they cannot fulfil their purpose' -- collapses a widely-used binary that most school assessment policies still formally enshrine.
Myth 1 they dismantle: treating 'big tests' as purely bureaucratic measurement rather than asking how the test's existence can help students learn better.
Myth 2: the common claim that summative assessments need high accuracy while formative ones can be 'rough and ready' is false -- both require valid inferences to support the decisions riding on them.

AI-driven adaptive platforms (Sparx Maths, Duolingo) are offered as proof the formative/summative distinction has already collapsed in practice, since these tools assess and shape learning in the same real-time loop.
quotes: We argue that all assessments must be both formative and summative—otherwise, they cannot fulfil their purpose. And what is their purpose? To promote learning.
An assessment is formative if it informs teaching and learning. It is summative if it is used to make judgments about attainment.

If we believe that only formative assessments contribute to learning, we risk treating larger, high-stakes tests as purely bureaucratic exercises—measuring attainment for a spreadsheet rather than supporting student progress.
All assessments require a reasonable degree of accuracy because decisions—whether in the moment or at the end of a course—depend on valid inferences.

Consider platforms like Sparx Maths or Duolingo. These tools maintain an ongoing picture of a student’s attainment based on responses to questions which could equally be used to predict future performance or generate short term personalised learning goals.
Relying on the words summative and formative leads to dysfunctional assessment practices in schools.
